items.item: Atomicity and ordering are genuinely separable: a program can have perfect atomicity (every individual read or write is indivisible) while still having zero ordering guarantee between threads about when those writes become visible.

items.item: A relaxed fetch_add across many threads never loses or tears an update, no matter how much contention there is on the same atomic location — demonstrated directly by an exact, repeatable final count.

items.item: The relaxed publication pattern (store data, then store a ready flag, both Relaxed; another thread checks the flag then reads the data) is unsound: nothing stops a reader from observing the flag as set before observing the data write, because Relaxed creates no happens-before edge between the two threads.

items.item: A tool like loom proves this kind of violation by exhaustively exploring every interleaving the memory model actually permits, rather than relying on a specific run's hardware behavior happening to expose (or hide) the bug.

items.item: Rust's atomics are explicitly specified to follow the C++20 memory model, with one named exception: the 'consume' ordering, which C++20 itself never finished specifying well enough to be relied on.

at.step: The missing piece has a name: happens-before

items.item: Happens-before is the foundational relation the whole model is built from: every one of Rust's orderings (Relaxed, Release, Acquire, AcqRel, SeqCst) is defined in terms of what happens-before edges it does or doesn't create.

at.step: The missing piece has a name: happens-before

items.item: A data race has a precise technical definition, not a vague one: conflicting (overlapping, at least one a write) accesses to the same memory with no happens-before relation between them — and Rust, like C++20, treats this as undefined behavior, not merely an incorrect value.

at.step: Unsynchronized conflicting access is undefined behavior, full stop

items.item: Undefined behavior is a stronger claim than 'the output might be wrong': it means the compiler is permitted to assume a data race never happens and optimize accordingly, which can produce effects with no sensible relationship to the source code at all.

at.step: Unsynchronized conflicting access is undefined behavior, full stop

items.item: The Linux kernel maintains its own, separately-specified memory model (LKMM), distinct from and in places stricter than the C++20-derived model this chapter covers, because the kernel's concurrency primitives and constraints differ from ordinary userspace Rust.

at.step: The kernel has its own, stricter model — and it only matters in the kernel

items.item: Choosing an ordering is not a performance-only decision with no correctness consequence: picking Relaxed where Acquire/Release or SeqCst was actually needed produces a program that is incorrect, not merely slower, even though it may appear to work on any given run.

at.step: Recap: atomicity and ordering, each proven separately
